partner_context.their_ambition: London already runs a 24-pier commuter River Bus network the length of the tidal Thames. Thames Clippers operates London's principal River Bus network (branded Uber Boat by Thames Clippers), coordinated with Transport for London as part of London's public transport. It runs the RB1/RB2/RB4/RB6 services across 24 piers between Putney in the west and Barking Riverside in the east, carrying millions of commuter and visitor journeys a year.
partner_context.their_pressure: Thames Clippers has launched the first hybrid-powered river buses on the Thames and is targeting zero-emission operation, aligned with London's 2030 net-zero goal. Growth and the net-zero mandate both demand fleet renewal without disturbing the services people rely on today.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined foiling upgrade to a river-bus network London already runs at commuter scale. Foiling hulls are faster and far lower-wash - important on the wake-restricted tidal Thames - and the speed advantage compounds on the longer east-London reaches toward Canary Wharf, Greenwich, Royal Wharf, Woolwich and Barking Riverside.

hero.title: Uber Boat by Thames Clippers × Navier — a zero-emission foiling layer on the water
hero.subtitle: A foiling tier above today's ferry network on the tidal Thames through London: faster, near-silent, low-wake lines, a clear decarbonization path, and the services people rely on left running underneath.
hero.what_we_do_together: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined foiling upgrade to a river-bus network London already runs at commuter scale. Foiling hulls are faster and far lower-wash - important on the wake-restricted tidal Thames - and the speed advantage compounds on the longer east-London reaches toward Canary Wharf, Greenwich, Royal Wharf, Woolwich and Barking Riverside.

why_now: A zero-emission foiling tier is the fast, low-wake fleet renewal the river bus needs - faster than the current catamarans, near-silent and low-wash for the tidal Thames, advancing London's 2030 net-zero target. Thames Clippers has launched the first hybrid-powered river buses on the Thames and is targeting zero-emission operation, aligned with London's 2030 net-zero goal. A demo vessel is on the water now.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the network as the fast marine mode on the tidal Thames through London — feeding the existing rail, metro and bus interchanges and adding lines toward the authority's published growth and net-zero targets.

objections.concern: Can a foiling boat work on the wash-restricted, bridge-lined Thames?
objections.response: Yes — it runs displacement and low-wash through the central bridge spans and the moorings, with foiling reserved for the wider, clearer east-London reaches where the PLA permits. The speed advantage compounds toward Docklands and Woolwich.
Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing piers — no new shore power, vertiports or rights-of-way.

objections.concern: Is foiling safe in busy, shared public waterways?
objections.response: Foiling is software-governed — geofenced no-foil and low-wake zones near piers, ferry lanes and moorings, automatic speed and wake limits in shared water, and conventional low-speed handling everywhere it isn't cleared to fly.

close.title: A zero-emission water layer that grows with the city.
close.body: Start on the busiest commuter corridors, scale across the full the tidal Thames through London network, then mature the service — a zero-emission foiling tier that advances the authority's net-zero mandate while the services people rely on keep running underneath.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the open water and the piers already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the long-range hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all. Nothing to permit, build, or wait for.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the charging excuse. Autonomy is arriving on the water before the road. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
